message.content:
# Introduction

Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) have fundamentally transformed the landscape of machine learning research, particularly in the domain of natural language processing [a field that {historically (relied upon (statistical (approaches) that were computationally intensive and heavily dependent on hand-engineered features) but now leverages} transformer-based architectures capable of scaling to unprecedented model sizes]. This paradigm shift has enabled systems to achieve near-human or superhuman performance on a range of standardized benchmarks, raising profound questions about the nature of machine understanding, the limits of generalization in high-dimensional representation spaces, and the epistemological status of patterns that emerge from large-scale parametric optimization.

The current trajectory of research is shaped by two competing tensions. On one hand, the scaling hypothesis suggests that emergent capabilities—such as in-context learning, chain-of-thought reasoning, and few-shot adaptation—are direct consequences of increasing model scale, data volume, and compute budget. On the other hand, growing evidence of systematic failure modes, including hallucination, sensitivity to prompt phrasing, and opaque internal representations, has motivated a parallel line of inquiry focused on interpretability, mechanistic analysis, and the design of architectures that are inherently more aligned with human values.

This paper contributes to the latter effort by proposing a unified framework for analyzing the relationship between architectural inductive biases and emergent reasoning behavior. We argue that the apparent unpredictability of large language models arises not from a fundamental limit on learnability but from a mismatch between the optimization landscape of next-token prediction and the compositional structure of human language—a mismatch that can be partially resolved through targeted architectural modifications. Our results, drawn from controlled experiments across three model families and two orders of magnitude in scale, suggest that even modest changes to attention masking and positional encoding yield measurable improvements in consistency and factuality without significant degradation on standard perplexity metrics.
